main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic English language skills
specific_competence_name: Develop vocabulary by relating words with objects in the environment
learning_activity_name: Find synonyms and antonyms of targeted words in different texts
sla_name: Identifying antonyms (opposite words)
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly gives the antonym for at least six words such as hot-cold, happy-sad, and big-small.
sla_teaching_aids: Word cards|Pictures of elephants of different sizes|Chalkboard|Exercise books
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Words that mean the opposite of one another are known as antonyms. For example, the antonym of hot is cold, and the antonym of happy is sad.
sla_notes_details: Pupils look at pictures, such as two elephants of different sizes, answer questions comparing them, and then name the opposite word for size, for example the opposite of small is huge, large or big. Knowing antonyms helps pupils speak and write more clearly and understand what others say more easily.
sla_notes_illustrations: Examples from the book include hot-cold, happy-sad and big-small. Pupils also practise finding antonyms of words used in giving directions, such as left and right, and in front of and behind.
sla_notes_daily_life: Knowing antonyms helps a pupil describe things more precisely at home and in the community, for example telling a young sibling that a path is short instead of not long.
sla_exercise: What is the antonym of small?::The antonym of small is big, huge or large.||What is the antonym of happy?::The antonym of happy is sad.||What is the antonym of hot?::The antonym of hot is cold.||What is the antonym of left as used in giving directions?::The antonym of left is right.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic English language skills
specific_competence_name: Develop vocabulary by relating words with objects in the environment
learning_activity_name: Find synonyms and antonyms of targeted words in different texts
sla_name: Identifying synonyms (same-meaning words)
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly gives at least three synonyms for a given word such as big, large and huge.
sla_teaching_aids: Word cards|Pictures of tall buildings|Chalkboard|Exercise books
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Words with the same or almost identical meanings are known as synonyms. For example, big and large are synonyms because they both describe something of great size.
sla_notes_details: Pupils look at pictures of buildings and describe their height, then name other words that mean the same thing. Learning synonyms helps pupils enrich their vocabulary, make their speaking and writing more interesting, and say the same thing in different ways.
sla_notes_illustrations: Examples from the book include big-large-huge, happy-joyful-glad and fast-quick-speedy.
sla_notes_daily_life: Using synonyms helps a pupil avoid repeating the same word when describing something to family members, for example switching between big and huge when talking about a new building in the village.
sla_exercise: What are two synonyms of the word happy?::Two synonyms of happy are joyful and glad.||What are two synonyms of the word fast?::Two synonyms of fast are quick and speedy.||What is a synonym of the word big?::A synonym of big is large or huge.||Why is it useful to know synonyms?::Knowing synonyms helps a person say the same thing in different ways and makes speech and writing more interesting.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic English language skills
specific_competence_name: Develop vocabulary by relating words with objects in the environment
learning_activity_name: Find synonyms and antonyms of targeted words in different texts
sla_name: Using synonyms and antonyms in songs, poems and passages
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly identifies at least four synonym or antonym pairs from a song or poem after singing or reciting it.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Synonyms and antonyms can be found and practised through songs and poems, which make learning new vocabulary enjoyable and memorable.
sla_notes_details: In the song 'Come and Learn', pupils identify synonyms of words like happy, big, fast and connect, and antonyms of words like small, slow, sad and lift. In the poem 'Human beings are different', pupils list pairs of words with opposite meanings that describe how people and their bodies differ, such as tall-short and fat-slim.
sla_notes_illustrations: From the song: a synonym of happy can be glad, and the antonym of small is big or large. From the poem: examples of antonym pairs are neat-messy, kind-rude, tall-short and heavy-light.
sla_notes_daily_life: Singing and reciting with synonyms and antonyms helps a pupil remember new words easily and use them confidently in everyday conversation.
sla_exercise: According to the song 'Come and Learn', what is a synonym of the word happy?::A synonym of happy is glad.||According to the song, what is the antonym of the word small?::The antonym of small is big.||From the poem 'Human beings are different', name one pair of antonyms describing body size.::One pair is tall and short.||From the poem, name one pair of antonyms describing behaviour.::One pair is kind and rude.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic English language skills
specific_competence_name: Develop vocabulary by relating words with objects in the environment
learning_activity_name: Solve word puzzles from various media
sla_name: Solving a crossword word puzzle
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil circles at least five meaningful words from a word puzzle and pronounces them correctly.
sla_teaching_aids: Printed word puzzle grid|Coloured pens|Chalkboard|Exercise books
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A word puzzle is a grid of letters in which meaningful words are hidden and must be found by searching across, down or diagonally.
sla_notes_details: Pupils study a word puzzle carefully, circle at least ten meaningful words such as broiler, poultry, eggs, snow and graduation, and practise pronouncing each word correctly. This exercise builds vocabulary recognition and spelling awareness.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example words found in the book's puzzle include broiler, poultry, eggs and graduation, hidden among rows of scrambled letters.
sla_notes_daily_life: Solving word puzzles helps a pupil build patience and vocabulary that can be used when reading newspapers, magazines or puzzle books at home.
sla_exercise: What is a word puzzle?::A word puzzle is a grid of letters containing hidden meaningful words that must be found and circled.||Name one meaningful word that can be found in the book's word puzzle.::One example is poultry.||Name another meaningful word found in the book's word puzzle.::Another example is graduation.||Why should you practise pronouncing the words you find?::Practising pronunciation helps you say the words correctly and remember their meaning.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic English language skills
specific_competence_name: Develop vocabulary by relating words with objects in the environment
learning_activity_name: Solve word puzzles from various media
sla_name: Finding meaningful words and using them in sentences
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil writes one correct sentence for each of at least three words found in a word puzzle.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: After finding meaningful words in a puzzle, pupils show they understand each word by using it correctly in a sentence.
sla_notes_details: For every word circled in the puzzle, such as eggs or poultry, a pupil writes down synonym and antonym pairs where possible, and then constructs one clear sentence to demonstrate its meaning.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example: for the word 'eggs', a pupil may write 'We collected eggs from the poultry this morning.'
sla_notes_daily_life: Using new words in sentences helps a pupil remember them and apply them when writing letters or describing daily activities at home.
sla_exercise: Write a sentence using the word poultry.::We keep poultry in a small house behind our home.||Write a sentence using the word eggs.::The hen laid five eggs yesterday.||Write a sentence using the word graduation.::My sister will attend her graduation next month.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic English language skills
specific_competence_name: Develop vocabulary by relating words with objects in the environment
learning_activity_name: Solve word puzzles from various media
sla_name: Creating and solving personal word puzzles
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil finds or creates a word puzzle and correctly identifies and explains at least five meaningful words in it.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Word puzzles can also be found in newspapers, magazines or online sources, and pupils can practise finding and solving them independently.
sla_notes_details: Pupils look for a crossword puzzle in a newspaper, magazine or online source, solve it, and write down five meaningful words found. For each word, they write one good sentence to show they understand its meaning.
sla_notes_illustrations: A pupil may find the word 'library' in a newspaper puzzle and write the sentence: 'I borrowed a storybook from the library.'
sla_notes_daily_life: Finding and solving puzzles from newspapers encourages a pupil to read more at home and improves their vocabulary over time.
sla_exercise: Where can you find word puzzles apart from your textbook?::Word puzzles can be found in newspapers, magazines or online sources.||After solving a puzzle, what should you do with each word you find?::You should write one good sentence to show that you understand its meaning.||Write a sentence using a word you found in a puzzle, for example market.::My mother sells vegetables at the market.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic English language skills
specific_competence_name: Develop vocabulary by relating words with objects in the environment
learning_activity_name: Construct short passages using vocabulary referring to objects found in different settings
sla_name: Filling gaps in a passage using vocabulary of feelings and school routines
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly fills at least six blanks in a passage about daily school routine using appropriate vocabulary.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A short passage can be completed by choosing the correct word from a table to describe feelings, people and school routines.
sla_notes_details: Pupils read a passage describing a school day and fill in blanks with words such as happy, teacher, smart, begin, end, big and small, making sure each sentence makes sense and is grammatically correct.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example completed sentence: 'I feel happy because I enjoy learning new things,' and 'We begin our lessons at 7:30 a.m. and end at 3:00 p.m.'
sla_notes_daily_life: Completing passages about daily routines helps a pupil describe their own school day clearly to parents or friends.
sla_exercise: Complete: I feel ______ because I enjoy learning new things.::I feel happy because I enjoy learning new things.||Complete: We ______ our lessons at 7:30 a.m.::We begin our lessons at 7:30 a.m.||Complete: Our classroom is ______, and we have space to move around.::Our classroom is big, and we have space to move around.||What word describes a library with no room for many people?::The word is small.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic English language skills
specific_competence_name: Develop vocabulary by relating words with objects in the environment
learning_activity_name: Construct short passages using vocabulary referring to objects found in different settings
sla_name: Rewriting a passage using antonyms
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil rewrites a given passage by correctly replacing at least four words with their opposite meaning.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A passage can be rewritten using antonyms of the words originally used, changing the meaning of the sentences while keeping them grammatically correct.
sla_notes_details: Pupils take the completed passage about the school day and replace words such as happy, big, early and begin with their opposites, such as sad, small, late and end, adjusting other words as needed so the passage still makes sense.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example: 'We begin our lessons at 7:30 a.m.' can be rewritten as 'We end our lessons at 7:30 a.m.' when practising the antonym of begin.
sla_notes_daily_life: Practising antonym rewriting helps a pupil vary their language when retelling the same event in different ways at home.
sla_exercise: Rewrite using an antonym: 'I feel happy because I enjoy learning.'::I feel sad because I do not enjoy learning.||Rewrite using an antonym: 'Our classroom is big.'::Our classroom is small.||What is the antonym of the word begin?::The antonym of begin is end.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic English language skills
specific_competence_name: Develop vocabulary by relating words with objects in the environment
learning_activity_name: Construct short passages using vocabulary referring to objects found in different settings
sla_name: Constructing an original short passage about objects in a setting
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil writes an original passage of at least four sentences describing objects found in a chosen setting, using correct vocabulary.
sla_teaching_aids: Pictures of different settings (home, school, market)|Chalkboard|Exercise books
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Pupils use the vocabulary they have learnt to write their own short passage describing objects found in a setting of their choice, such as their classroom, home or the market.
sla_notes_details: Each pupil chooses a setting, lists objects found there, and writes a short passage of four or more sentences describing those objects using suitable adjectives, synonyms or antonyms where appropriate.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example passage: 'My classroom is big and bright. There are wooden desks and a large chalkboard. Our books are kept on a small shelf near the door.'
sla_notes_daily_life: Writing about objects in familiar settings helps a pupil describe their home or school clearly when writing a letter to a relative.
sla_exercise: Name one setting you could write a passage about.::One setting could be the classroom, the market or the home.||Write one sentence describing an object found in your classroom.::There is a large chalkboard at the front of our classroom.||Why is it useful to use synonyms and antonyms when writing a passage?::Using synonyms and antonyms makes a passage more interesting and shows a wider vocabulary.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic English language skills
specific_competence_name: Use appropriate grammar and vocabulary both orally and in writing
learning_activity_name: Compare things based on size, quality and quantity (e.g., big-bigger-biggest, much-more-most)
sla_name: Comparing size using comparatives and superlatives (big, bigger, biggest)
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly uses comparative and superlative forms to compare three objects, such as saying a rock is big, bigger and biggest.
sla_teaching_aids: Pictures of stones of different sizes|Pictures of trees of different heights|Chalkboard|Exercise books
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Comparatives show differences between two things, while superlatives show the highest or lowest quality among three or more things. For example, 'A ruler is longer than a pencil' uses a comparative, while 'Lake Victoria is the largest freshwater lake in Africa' uses a superlative.
sla_notes_details: Pupils look at three stones and three trees of different sizes and complete dialogues describing which is bigger, biggest, taller and tallest. They practise giving the three forms of adjectives such as big, bigger, biggest and small, smaller, smallest.
sla_notes_illustrations: In the story 'Comparisons on a walk', the first rock was big, the second was bigger, and the third was the biggest, while one tree was small, another smaller, and the last the smallest.
sla_notes_daily_life: Comparing the sizes of things helps a pupil describe which sibling is taller or which mango is bigger when sharing at home.
sla_exercise: What is the comparative form of the word big?::The comparative form of big is bigger.||What is the superlative form of the word small?::The superlative form of small is smallest.||In the story, which rock was the biggest?::The third rock was the biggest.||Write the three forms of the word tall.::The three forms are tall, taller, tallest.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic English language skills
specific_competence_name: Use appropriate grammar and vocabulary both orally and in writing
learning_activity_name: Compare things based on size, quality and quantity (e.g., big-bigger-biggest, much-more-most)
sla_name: Comparing quantity and quality using more...than and most
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly compares the quantity or quality of at least three items using 'more...than' and 'the most'.
sla_teaching_aids: Pictures of books, pens and animals|Pictures of animals and houses|Chalkboard|Exercise books
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: We use 'more...than' to compare the quantity of two or more things, and words like 'more powerful' or 'the most beautiful' to compare their quality.
sla_notes_details: Pupils compare quantities, such as there being more pens in a pocket than books on a table, and more animals than both. They also compare quality, for example saying an elephant is more powerful than a lion, and deciding which of three houses is the most beautiful.
sla_notes_illustrations: From the dialogue: there are four animals, three pens, and two books, so there are more animals than pens or books. From the animal comparison: the elephant is more powerful than the lion, but the elephant is the most powerful of the three animals shown.
sla_notes_daily_life: Comparing quantity and quality helps a pupil decide which shop sells more items or which food tastes better when helping with shopping at home.
sla_exercise: Which has more, the pocket with three pens or the table with two books?::The pocket has more pens than the table has books.||Which animal is more powerful, the elephant or the lion?::The elephant is more powerful than the lion.||Which of the three houses is the most beautiful?::The house judged most beautiful is the one with the best combination of features, for example house C.||What word do we add before an adjective to compare more than two things at the highest degree?::We use the word 'most' before the adjective.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic English language skills
specific_competence_name: Use appropriate grammar and vocabulary both orally and in writing
learning_activity_name: Express location using appropriate prepositions of direction (target: towards, between, beside, from, into, onto, through, across)
sla_name: Using between and beside to describe location
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly describes the location of at least three objects using the prepositions between and beside.
sla_teaching_aids: Real classroom objects|Pictures of boxes and balls|Chalkboard
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Prepositions of location such as 'between' and 'beside' tell us exactly where an object is placed in relation to other objects.
sla_notes_details: Pupils look at pictures such as a ball placed between two boxes or beside one box, and answer questions about the position of objects like an apple, a plate and a cup, using between, beside, under and on.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example sentences from the book: 'The ball is between the boxes' and 'The ball is beside the box.'
sla_notes_daily_life: Using between and beside helps a pupil explain exactly where an item is kept at home, for example that the broom is beside the door.
sla_exercise: Where is the ball if it has two boxes on either side of it?::The ball is between the boxes.||Complete: The cow is ______ the tree.::The cow is beside the tree.||Complete: The boy is standing ______ the beds.::The boy is standing between the beds.||Complete: There is a flower vase ______ the table.::There is a flower vase beside the table.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic English language skills
specific_competence_name: Use appropriate grammar and vocabulary both orally and in writing
learning_activity_name: Express location using appropriate prepositions of direction (target: towards, between, beside, from, into, onto, through, across)
sla_name: Using into, onto, through, across, towards and from to describe direction
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly uses at least four direction prepositions (into, onto, through, across, towards, from) in complete sentences.
sla_teaching_aids: Pictures showing movement (cat jumping, boy climbing, lion crossing road)|Chalkboard
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Prepositions such as 'into', 'onto', 'through', 'across', 'towards' and 'from' describe the direction in which someone or something moves.
sla_notes_details: Pupils study sentences and pictures such as 'The cat jumped into the box', 'The boy climbed onto the roof', 'The lion walked across the road', 'The rhino ran towards the car', and 'The boy walked away from the washroom', then answer questions about each.
sla_notes_illustrations: From the passage 'A visit to the village': Asha and Juma walked across a small bridge over the river, and Asha went into the kitchen to help with cooking.
sla_notes_daily_life: Using these prepositions helps a pupil give clear directions when telling someone how to walk from home to school, for example walking across the field and through the gate.
sla_exercise: Complete: The cat jumped ______ the box.::The cat jumped into the box.||Complete: The boy ran ______ the river to reach the other side.::The boy ran across the river to reach the other side.||Complete: He came ______ school with a big smile.::He came from school with a big smile.||Complete: The cow walked slowly ______ the farmer.::The cow walked slowly towards the farmer.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic English language skills
specific_competence_name: Use appropriate grammar and vocabulary both orally and in writing
learning_activity_name: Express possession using adjectives and pronouns (target: my, mine, yours, his, her, hers, their, theirs)
sla_name: Using possessive adjectives (my, your, his, her, its, our, their)
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly uses at least five possessive adjectives to complete sentences about ownership.
sla_teaching_aids: Pictures of family members and belongings|Chalkboard|Exercise books
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Possessive adjectives are special words used to show who owns something, such as my, your, his, her, its, our and their.
sla_notes_details: Pupils construct sentences using each possessive adjective, such as 'This is my book' or 'That is their car', following the table of personal pronouns and their matching possessive adjectives. They also identify possessive words used in a dialogue and a passage about family and friends.
sla_notes_illustrations: From the dialogue between Rehema and David: 'My name is David. I have a brother; his name is Adam' and 'They used their long-term savings.'
sla_notes_daily_life: Using possessive adjectives correctly helps a pupil clearly tell others whose belongings are whose at home or school, avoiding confusion.
sla_exercise: Complete using a possessive adjective: This is ______ book. (I)::This is my book.||Complete using a possessive adjective: The dog is eating ______ food. (it)::The dog is eating its food.||Complete using a possessive adjective: That is ______ car. (they)::That is their car.||In the dialogue, what does David call his brother's name using a possessive adjective?::David says 'his name is Adam.'

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic English language skills
specific_competence_name: Use appropriate grammar and vocabulary both orally and in writing
learning_activity_name: Express possession using adjectives and pronouns (target: my, mine, yours, his, her, hers, their, theirs)
sla_name: Using possessive pronouns (mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs)
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly rewrites at least four sentences using possessive pronouns to avoid repeating the noun.
sla_teaching_aids: Pictures of a wheelchair, bag and school|Chalkboard|Exercise books
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Possessive pronouns such as mine, yours, his, hers, its, ours and theirs replace nouns in sentences and show who possesses what.
sla_notes_details: Pupils rewrite sentences that describe ownership, such as 'The wheelchair belongs to Mr Jumbe' becoming 'It is his', and 'The bag belongs to Jane' becoming 'It is hers'. They also convert other sentences such as 'That bicycle belongs to John' into 'That bicycle is his.'
sla_notes_illustrations: Example from the book: 'This is my family. This is our house. The house is ours' and 'This is a school. It is their school. It is theirs.'
sla_notes_daily_life: Using possessive pronouns helps a pupil answer quickly and clearly when asked whose item something is, without repeating the full name of the object.
sla_exercise: Rewrite using a possessive pronoun: 'That bicycle belongs to John.'::That bicycle is his.||Rewrite using a possessive pronoun: 'This house belongs to us.'::This house is ours.||Rewrite using a possessive pronoun: 'Those pairs of shoes belong to you.'::Those pairs of shoes are yours.||Whose wheelchair is it if it belongs to Mr Jumbe?::It is his.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic English language skills
specific_competence_name: Use appropriate grammar and vocabulary both orally and in writing
learning_activity_name: Express completed and unfinished actions (structure: present perfect, past perfect tense)
sla_name: Expressing completed actions using present perfect tense (has/have)
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly constructs at least four sentences using has or have to describe a completed action.
sla_teaching_aids: Pictures of a boy kicking a ball and a girl finishing a race|Chalkboard|Exercise books
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The present perfect tense, formed with has or have plus a past participle, is used to describe actions that have just been completed.
sla_notes_details: Pupils look at pictures of a boy who has kicked a ball and a girl who has finished a race, and answer questions using has and have correctly. They also practise choosing has or have to complete sentences such as 'Mary and Moses ______ eaten the food.'
sla_notes_illustrations: Example from the book: 'The boy has kicked the ball' and 'The girl has finished the race.'
sla_notes_daily_life: Using the present perfect tense helps a pupil report to a parent or teacher what task they have just completed, such as 'I have finished my homework.'
sla_exercise: Complete: The boy ______ kicked the ball. (has/have)::The boy has kicked the ball.||Complete: Mary and Moses ______ eaten the food. (has/have)::Mary and Moses have eaten the food.||Change into a question: 'She has scored a brilliant goal.'::Has she scored a brilliant goal?||Complete: The thief ______ stolen my school bag.::The thief has stolen my school bag.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic English language skills
specific_competence_name: Use appropriate grammar and vocabulary both orally and in writing
learning_activity_name: Express completed and unfinished actions (structure: present perfect, past perfect tense)
sla_name: Expressing unfinished actions using present perfect continuous (has/have been)
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly forms at least two sentences using has/have been plus a verb with -ing to describe an action that started in the past and continues.
sla_teaching_aids: Pictures of Juma watering a garden|Chalkboard|Exercise books
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The present perfect continuous tense, formed with has or have been plus a verb ending in -ing, describes an action that started in the past and is still happening now.
sla_notes_details: Pupils study pictures of Juma watering a garden from 06:00 pm to 06:30 pm and answer questions such as 'What has Juma been doing?' They also read a dialogue between Sadick and Anna about a book Sadick started reading last month but has not finished.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example from the dialogue: 'I have been reading this book since last month' means Sadick started reading the book last month and is still reading it.
sla_notes_daily_life: This tense helps a pupil explain an ongoing task to a parent, for example saying 'I have been doing my homework since four o'clock.'
sla_exercise: What has Juma been doing since 06:00 pm?::Juma has been watering the garden.||Complete: Tausi ______ planting flowers since morning. (has/have been)::Tausi has been planting flowers since morning.||Why does Sadick say 'I have been reading this book since last month'?::He says this because he started reading the book last month and has still not finished it.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic English language skills
specific_competence_name: Use appropriate grammar and vocabulary both orally and in writing
learning_activity_name: Express completed and unfinished actions (structure: present perfect, past perfect tense)
sla_name: Expressing past completed actions using past perfect tense (had)
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly constructs at least two sentences using had plus a past participle to show one past action happened before another.
sla_teaching_aids: Clock face pictures|Time and action table|Chalkboard|Exercise books
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The past perfect tense, formed with had plus a past participle, shows that one action in the past happened before another past action.
sla_notes_details: Pupils use a table of times and actions, such as James eating breakfast at 10:05 am before his father came home at 12:10 pm, to write sentences like 'James had eaten breakfast before his father came home.' They also change present perfect sentences into past perfect, such as 'Ashura has locked the door' becoming 'Ashura had locked the door.'
sla_notes_illustrations: Example from the book: 'The boy had cleaned the blackboard before the teacher wrote the word English.'
sla_notes_daily_life: Using the past perfect tense helps a pupil explain the correct order of events when narrating what happened before a visitor arrived at home.
sla_exercise: Complete: Mary ______ cleaned her room before her friend arrived. (had)::Mary had cleaned her room before her friend arrived.||Change to past perfect: 'Ashura has locked the door.'::Ashura had locked the door.||Complete: Naomi ______ finished writing before John cleaned the board.::Naomi had finished writing before John cleaned the board.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic English language skills
specific_competence_name: Use appropriate grammar and vocabulary both orally and in writing
learning_activity_name: Use conjunctions in oral and written contexts (target: too… to, either …or, neither…nor)
sla_name: Using either...or to express a choice
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly joins two sentences into one using either...or to show a choice between two things.
sla_teaching_aids: Pictures of a banana and an apple, a red and a blue blouse|Chalkboard
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The conjunction 'either...or' suggests making one choice between two things, persons or conditions.
sla_notes_details: Pupils study example sentences such as 'The boy can choose to eat either a banana or an apple' and 'The girl can choose to wear either a red or a blue blouse', then describe the choices given in similar sentences and construct their own.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example from the book: 'Either Baraka or Zawadi will clean the window' means one of these two will clean the window.
sla_notes_daily_life: Using either...or helps a pupil offer a choice clearly when asking a family member what they would prefer to eat or wear.
sla_exercise: Join using either...or: 'You can stay. You can also leave.'::You can either stay or leave.||What are the two choices in: 'Janeth needs either a pen or a pencil to do her homework'?::The two choices are a pen and a pencil.||Complete: You can eat ______ rice ______ ugali.::You can eat either rice or ugali.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic English language skills
specific_competence_name: Use appropriate grammar and vocabulary both orally and in writing
learning_activity_name: Use conjunctions in oral and written contexts (target: too… to, either …or, neither…nor)
sla_name: Using neither...nor to express two negatives
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly joins two negative sentences into one using neither...nor.
sla_teaching_aids: Pictures of a sleeping dog and cat, rotten bananas and apples|Chalkboard
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The conjunction 'neither...nor' joins two negative alternatives, meaning that neither of the two things is true or possible.
sla_notes_details: Pupils study examples such as 'The child can eat neither bananas nor apples because they are rotten' and 'Neither the dog nor the cat is awake', then split similar sentences back into two separate negative sentences and combine given negative sentences using neither...nor.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example from the book: 'Neither Bakari nor James opened the window' means Bakari did not open the window, and James did not open the window either.
sla_notes_daily_life: Using neither...nor helps a pupil clearly state that two options are both unavailable, for example telling a friend that neither the shop nor the market had sugar.
sla_exercise: Join using neither...nor: 'She is not talkative. She is not reserved.'::She is neither talkative nor reserved.||Split into two sentences: 'Neither the dog nor the cat wants to eat.'::The dog does not want to eat. The cat does not want to eat either.||Join using neither...nor: 'She does not like ugali. She does not like rice.'::She likes neither ugali nor rice.||Join using neither...nor: 'We had not taken umbrellas. We had not taken raincoats.'::We had taken neither umbrellas nor raincoats.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic English language skills
specific_competence_name: Use appropriate grammar and vocabulary both orally and in writing
learning_activity_name: Use conjunctions in oral and written contexts (target: too… to, either …or, neither…nor)
sla_name: Using too...to to express a limitation
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly joins two sentences into one using too...to to show that something cannot be done because of a limitation.
sla_teaching_aids: Pictures of a heavy desk and a short boy near a mango tree|Chalkboard
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The conjunction 'too...to' shows that something has too much of a quality to allow an action to happen, such as being too heavy to lift.
sla_notes_details: Pupils study examples like 'The desk is too heavy to lift' and 'The boy is too short to pick the mangoes from the tree', then join pairs of sentences describing a quality and its resulting limitation into one sentence using too...to.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example from the book: 'The water is very cold. He can't drink it' becomes 'The water is too cold to drink.'
sla_notes_daily_life: Using too...to helps a pupil explain why they cannot do a chore, for example saying the bucket is too heavy to carry alone.
sla_exercise: Join using too...to: 'The food is very hot. They can't eat it.'::The food is too hot to eat.||Join using too...to: 'I am very busy. I cannot talk to them.'::I am too busy to talk to them.||Join using too...to: 'The questions are very difficult. I cannot answer them.'::The questions are too difficult to answer.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic English language skills
specific_competence_name: Use appropriate grammar and vocabulary both orally and in writing
learning_activity_name: Use active and passive voices to communicate in different contexts
sla_name: Changing sentences from active to passive voice
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly changes at least four active voice sentences into passive voice.
sla_teaching_aids: Table of active and passive sentences|Chalkboard|Exercise books
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The active voice focuses on the doer of an action, while the passive voice shifts the focus to the receiver of the action.
sla_notes_details: Pupils study a table comparing active and passive sentences, such as 'The chef cooks the food' becoming 'The food is cooked by the chef', and practise transforming further sentences and questions such as 'Does the chef cook the food?' into 'Is the food cooked by the chef?'
sla_notes_illustrations: Example from the book: 'The boy kicked the ball' (active) becomes 'The ball was kicked by the boy' (passive).
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding passive voice helps a pupil describe events when the doer is unknown or unimportant, such as saying 'The window was broken' when reporting an accident at home.
sla_exercise: Change to passive voice: 'The dog chased the cat.'::The cat was chased by the dog.||Change to passive voice: 'The pupils answered the questions.'::The questions were answered by the pupils.||Change to passive voice: 'They will clean the room.'::The room will be cleaned by them.||Change to a passive question: 'Does the chef cook the food?'::Is the food cooked by the chef?

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of basic English language skills
specific_competence_name: Use appropriate grammar and vocabulary both orally and in writing
learning_activity_name: Use active and passive voices to communicate in different contexts
sla_name: Using active and passive voice in stories and interviews
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly identifies at least three passive voice sentences in a text and rewrites them in active voice.
sla_teaching_aids: Story text: Mr Fungo and the community|Interview extract|Chalkboard
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Active and passive voice are both used in real texts such as stories and interviews, often to hide or reveal who performed an action.
sla_notes_details: In the story 'Mr Fungo and the community', people avoid blaming Mr Fungo directly by using passive sentences such as 'The tap was damaged' and 'A mistake was made', instead of naming the doer. Pupils identify such passive sentences and change them into the active voice, and also examine active and passive sentences in an interview extract about a musician.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example from the story: 'The tap was damaged when the car was reversed' can be changed to 'The car damaged the tap when it was reversed.'
sla_notes_daily_life: Recognising when passive voice is used to avoid naming someone helps a pupil understand the true meaning of statements they hear in the community or in news reports.
sla_exercise: Who damaged the village water tap in the story?::Mr Fungo damaged the village water tap while reversing his lorry.||Change to active voice: 'The tap was repaired by Mr Fungo.'::Mr Fungo repaired the tap.||Change to active voice: 'He is called a man of the people in the community.'::The community calls him a man of the people.||Why did some people in the community use passive sentences like 'A mistake was made'?::They used passive sentences to avoid saying directly that Mr Fungo made the mistake.

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Comprehend information presented orally
learning_activity_name: Follow oral instructions to accomplish a task (e.g., operating equipment and making objects)
sla_name: Following oral instructions to operate a radio
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly follows at least four oral instructions to turn on a radio, adjust its volume and tune to a station.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Listening carefully to spoken instructions and carrying them out in the correct order is an important everyday listening skill.
sla_notes_details: Pupils listen to instructions such as finding the power button, pressing it to turn the radio on, turning the volume knob from left to right to increase the volume, using the tuning knob to find a station, and pressing the power button again to turn it off, then perform each step in order.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example instruction sequence from the book: press the power button to turn on the radio; turn the volume knob to increase the volume; use the tuning knob to find your favourite station.
sla_notes_daily_life: Following instructions to operate a radio helps a pupil safely use similar devices such as a family radio or music player at home.
sla_exercise: What should you press first to turn on a radio?::You should press the power button first.||How do you increase the volume on a radio?::You turn the volume knob from left to right.||What knob helps you find your favourite radio station?::The tuning knob helps you find your favourite station.||Why should you turn off the radio when not in use?::Turning it off saves energy and keeps the radio safe.

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Comprehend information presented orally
learning_activity_name: Follow oral instructions to accomplish a task (e.g., operating equipment and making objects)
sla_name: Following oral instructions to operate a phone or camera
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly follows oral instructions to turn on a device and take a simple photograph.
sla_teaching_aids: A phone or camera (real or picture)|Instruction cards|Chalkboard
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Oral instructions can also guide a pupil in operating other simple devices such as a torch, phone or camera.
sla_notes_details: Pupils listen to and follow instructions on how to take photos and record videos using a camera, phone or tablet, including pressing the correct button to turn the device on, checking that the subject is in focus, and pressing the shutter button to take the photo.
sla_notes_illustrations: Guiding questions from the book include: What button do we press to turn the camera on? What should you do before pressing the shutter button?
sla_notes_daily_life: Learning to follow instructions for using a phone or camera helps a pupil safely take family photographs during celebrations at home.
sla_exercise: What should you press to turn on a camera?::You should press the power button to turn on the camera.||What should you check before pressing the shutter button?::You should check that the subject is in focus.||Name one gadget on which you can practise setting an alarm.::You can practise setting an alarm on a mobile phone, an alarm clock or a digital watch.||Why is it useful to know how to use a camera or phone?::It helps you take photos and videos to record important moments in daily life.

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Comprehend information presented orally
learning_activity_name: Follow oral instructions to accomplish a task (e.g., operating equipment and making objects)
sla_name: Following oral instructions to make a paper craft
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly follows oral instructions to create one paper craft or piece of stone and sand art.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Following spoken instructions step by step allows a pupil to create simple objects such as paper crafts, stone art or sand art.
sla_notes_details: Pupils look at pictures of pupils making paper crafts and listen to instructions describing each step, then create their own paper craft. They also listen to instructions for making stone and sand art, such as a small garden, and follow the steps to make one.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example guiding question from the book: What is the first step in making a small garden? What are the other steps in making a small garden?
sla_notes_daily_life: Following instructions to make simple crafts helps a pupil create decorations or toys at home using locally available materials.
sla_exercise: What should you do after listening to instructions for a craft?::You should follow the instructions step by step to create the object.||Name one material you could use to make sand art.::You could use sand and small stones.||Why is it important to listen carefully before starting a craft?::Listening carefully helps you follow the correct order of steps and avoid mistakes.||What can you do with a finished paper craft?::You can display it in a visible area to show your creativity.

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Comprehend information presented orally
learning_activity_name: Listen to grade-appropriate myths, fairy tales and fables presented through audio/audiovisual channels and respond accordingly
sla_name: Listening to the fable Grandmother's Pumpkin and responding to questions
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil listens to the fable and correctly answers at least three comprehension questions about its characters and message.
sla_teaching_aids: Story text: Grandmother's Pumpkin|Pictures of a pumpkin and a hare|Chalkboard
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A fable is a short story, often with animal characters, that teaches a lesson about behaviour.
sla_notes_details: Pupils listen to the fable 'Grandmother's Pumpkin', in which a hare tries to steal a bite of Mama Siti's giant pumpkin instead of asking for a share, finds the skin too tough to bite, and is caught and forgiven by Mama Siti, learning that it is better to ask than to steal.
sla_notes_illustrations: Key events: the hare admires the pumpkin, waits until Mama Siti leaves, bites the tough skin, and is caught; Mama Siti says 'the pumpkin was meant for sharing, not stealing.'
sla_notes_daily_life: This fable teaches a pupil to ask permission before taking something that belongs to someone else, whether at home, school or in the neighbourhood.
sla_exercise: Who tried to take a bite of Mama Siti's pumpkin without asking?::The hare tried to take a bite of the pumpkin without asking.||Why was the hare unable to enjoy the pumpkin?::The pumpkin skin was too tough to bite.||What lesson did the hare learn at the end of the story?::The hare learned that it is better to ask for what you want than to steal.

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Comprehend information presented orally
learning_activity_name: Listen to grade-appropriate myths, fairy tales and fables presented through audio/audiovisual channels and respond accordingly
sla_name: Listening to a fairy tale and predicting what happens next
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil listens to part of a fairy tale and correctly predicts a reasonable next event, then confirms it after hearing the rest of the story.
sla_teaching_aids: Fairy tale audio or read-aloud text|Picture cards|Chalkboard
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A fairy tale is a traditional story, often involving magic or extraordinary characters, told to entertain and teach a lesson.
sla_notes_details: Pupils listen to a fairy tale, such as one about a poor girl who is kind to a stranger and is later rewarded, pausing partway through to predict what might happen next based on clues in the story, before listening to the ending to check their prediction.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, after hearing that a girl shares her last piece of bread with an old woman on the road, pupils predict that the old woman may reward the girl's kindness later in the story.
sla_notes_daily_life: Predicting what happens next in a story helps a pupil think ahead and reason about cause and effect in real-life situations, such as guessing the outcome of an action before it happens.
sla_exercise: What is a fairy tale?::A fairy tale is a traditional story, often with magic or extraordinary characters, told to entertain and teach a lesson.||Why is it useful to predict what will happen next in a story?::It helps a listener think ahead, pay closer attention, and check their understanding when the story continues.||If a character in a story is kind to a stranger, what might you predict will happen later?::You might predict that the character will be rewarded for their kindness later in the story.

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Comprehend information presented orally
learning_activity_name: Listen to grade-appropriate myths, fairy tales and fables presented through audio/audiovisual channels and respond accordingly
sla_name: Listening to a myth and retelling its moral lesson
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil listens to a myth and correctly states its moral lesson in their own words.
sla_teaching_aids: Myth text or audio|Pictures related to the myth|Chalkboard
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A myth is a traditional story, often explaining natural events or the origin of something, passed down from earlier generations.
sla_notes_details: Pupils listen to a myth, such as one explaining why the hare has long ears or why the tortoise has a cracked shell, identify the characters and events, and discuss the moral or explanation the myth gives.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a myth may explain that the tortoise's shell became cracked as a punishment for its pride, teaching listeners to remain humble.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding the moral lessons of myths helps a pupil apply values such as humility and honesty passed down through storytelling in their own community.
sla_exercise: What is a myth?::A myth is a traditional story, often explaining natural events or the origin of something.||What moral lesson can a myth about a proud animal teach?::It can teach that pride often leads to trouble and that one should remain humble.||Why do communities tell myths to children?::Communities tell myths to entertain children and to pass on important lessons and values.

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Comprehend information presented orally
learning_activity_name: Identify major and minor ideas in a story
sla_name: Identifying the main idea in the story Road Accident
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly identifies the main idea of the story 'Road Accident' from a set of options.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The main idea of a story is the single most important point that the whole story is about.
sla_notes_details: Pupils listen to the story 'Road accident', in which a schoolboy named Baraka Musa is hit by a car, identified through his exercise book, and taken to hospital by his father, then choose the sentence that best captures the whole story from a set of options.
sla_notes_illustrations: The correct main idea from the book is: 'A schoolboy had been hit by a car and rushed to hospital,' rather than smaller details like 'Baraka's father arrived by taxi.'
sla_notes_daily_life: Identifying the main idea helps a pupil quickly summarise what an announcement or news report on the radio was really about.
sla_exercise: What is the main idea of the story 'Road accident'?::The main idea is that a schoolboy had been hit by a car and rushed to hospital.||Is 'The bus stopped suddenly' the main idea or a supporting detail?::It is a supporting detail, not the main idea.||How was Baraka identified after the accident?::He was identified from the name written on his exercise book.

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Comprehend information presented orally
learning_activity_name: Identify major and minor ideas in a story
sla_name: Identifying supporting ideas (small details) in a story
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly identifies at least two supporting ideas that add detail to the main idea of a story.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Supporting ideas are smaller details that add extra information about the main idea of a story.
sla_notes_details: Pupils re-read the story 'Road accident' and pick out supporting ideas such as the boy's name being Baraka Musa, and that a phone number found in his exercise book was used to call his father, distinguishing these smaller details from the single main idea.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example supporting ideas from the book: 'The boy's name was Baraka Musa' and 'Baraka's father was called using a phone number found in the bag.'
sla_notes_daily_life: Noticing supporting details helps a pupil remember specific facts, such as names and numbers, when retelling news to family members.
sla_exercise: Give one supporting idea from the story 'Road accident'.::One supporting idea is that the boy's name was Baraka Musa.||How was Baraka's father contacted?::He was contacted using a phone number found inside Baraka's exercise book.||Why is 'A man opened Baraka's school bag' considered a supporting idea and not the main idea?::It is a small detail that helps the story but does not capture the whole story by itself.

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Comprehend information presented orally
learning_activity_name: Identify major and minor ideas in a story
sla_name: Distinguishing main ideas from minor ideas in a listened story
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly sorts a mixed list of story statements into one main idea and at least two supporting ideas.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Distinguishing between major and minor ideas means being able to tell which statement is the central point of a story and which statements only support it.
sla_notes_details: Using the fable 'Grandmother's pumpkin', pupils identify the sentence that best captures the whole story, such as the hare learning not to steal, and separate it from supporting details such as the pumpkin being bright orange or the hare being known for its speed.
sla_notes_illustrations: Main idea: the hare tries to steal from Mama Siti's garden and learns to ask instead. Supporting details: the pumpkin was the biggest Mama Siti had ever grown; the hare was known for high speed.
sla_notes_daily_life: Telling the difference between main and minor ideas helps a pupil focus on the important part of instructions given by a teacher or parent, rather than getting lost in small details.
sla_exercise: What is the main idea of the story 'Grandmother's pumpkin'?::The main idea is that the hare tried to steal but learned it is better to ask for what you want.||Give one supporting detail from the story 'Grandmother's pumpkin'.::One supporting detail is that the pumpkin was the biggest Mama Siti had ever grown.||Why is it useful to separate main ideas from minor ideas?::It helps a listener remember the most important message of a story without confusing it with smaller details.

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Comprehend information presented orally
learning_activity_name: Summarise issues found in the texts heard
sla_name: Predicting and summarising the content of a poem before and after listening
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil makes a reasonable prediction about a poem's content and then gives a one or two sentence summary after listening.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Before listening to a poem, pupils can predict what it might be about from its title and picture, and afterwards summarise what the poem was really about.
sla_notes_details: Pupils look at the title and picture of a poem and predict its topic, then listen carefully to the poem, noting how the opening lines make them feel and what they expect to happen next, before summarising the poem's overall message in their own words.
sla_notes_illustrations: Guiding questions from the book include: What do you think the poem will be about after hearing its title and looking at the picture? How do the first two lines make you feel?
sla_notes_daily_life: Predicting and summarising helps a pupil quickly grasp the message of songs or announcements they hear on the radio.
sla_exercise: What should you look at before predicting what a poem is about?::You should look at the poem's title and the picture that goes with it.||Why do we summarise a poem after listening to it?::We summarise a poem to show that we understood its overall message in our own words.||Give an example of a question you can ask yourself while listening to a poem.::An example is: What do I think will happen next in the poem?

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Comprehend information presented orally
learning_activity_name: Summarise issues found in the texts heard
sla_name: Summarising the main issue in a story heard
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil listens to a story and correctly gives a one or two sentence summary capturing its main issue.
sla_teaching_aids: Story text: Road accident or Grandmother's pumpkin|Chalkboard
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Summarising a story heard means shortening it into the fewest possible sentences while keeping its central issue and message.
sla_notes_details: After listening to a story such as 'Road accident', pupils summarise it by stating the main issue, for example that a schoolboy was hit by a car and later recovered, leaving out minor details like the exact time or side characters.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example summary: 'A schoolboy was hit by a car while crossing the road, was rushed to hospital, and later recovered.'
sla_notes_daily_life: Summarising helps a pupil report important news, such as an accident or event, to family members quickly and clearly.
sla_exercise: Give a one-sentence summary of the story 'Road accident'.::A schoolboy was hit by a car, rushed to hospital, and later recovered.||Give a one-sentence summary of the fable 'Grandmother's pumpkin'.::A hare tried to steal a pumpkin but learned it is better to ask than to steal.||What should a good summary of a story include?::A good summary should include the main issue of the story without unnecessary small details.

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Comprehend information presented orally
learning_activity_name: Summarise issues found in the texts heard
sla_name: Summarising a dialogue heard between two speakers
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil listens to a dialogue and correctly summarises what the two speakers agreed or talked about.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A dialogue can also be summarised by stating what the speakers were mainly talking about and what they decided or learned.
sla_notes_details: Pupils listen to the dialogue between Sadick and Anna about a book Sadick started reading last month but has not finished, and summarise it by stating that Anna helped Sadick learn how to express an action that started in the past and is still continuing.
sla_notes_illustrations: Summary example: Sadick was struggling to describe a book he started but had not finished, and Anna taught him to say 'I have been reading this book since last month.'
sla_notes_daily_life: Summarising conversations helps a pupil report what was discussed in a meeting or conversation to someone who was not present.
sla_exercise: What was Sadick struggling with in his conversation with Anna?::He was struggling to make a sentence about a book he started reading but had not finished.||What sentence did Anna teach Sadick to use?::Anna taught him to say 'I have been reading this book since last month.'||Give a one-sentence summary of the dialogue between Sadick and Anna.::Anna helped Sadick learn how to talk about an action that started in the past and is still continuing.

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Comprehend information presented orally
learning_activity_name: Retell oral texts
sla_name: Retelling a picture story in own words
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil retells a picture story in their own words, correctly mentioning the main characters and events.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Retelling means telling a story again in your own words after listening to or looking at it, keeping the important characters and events.
sla_notes_details: Pupils look at a picture and listen to a story about it, identifying the main characters, where and when it takes place, and what happens at the beginning, middle and end, then retell the story to a partner or the class in their own words.
sla_notes_illustrations: Guiding questions from the book include: Who are the main characters in the story? What happened at the beginning, middle and end of the story?
sla_notes_daily_life: Retelling stories helps a pupil share news or events they witnessed with family members in a clear and organised way.
sla_exercise: What should you identify before retelling a picture story?::You should identify the main characters, the setting, and what happens at the beginning, middle and end.||Why is it useful to retell a story in your own words?::It shows that you understood the story and helps others who did not hear it the first time.||What problem might characters face in a story, and how could it be solved?::Characters might face a problem such as losing something, which is solved by working together to find it.

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Comprehend information presented orally
learning_activity_name: Retell oral texts
sla_name: Retelling the fable Grandmother's Pumpkin
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly retells the fable 'Grandmother's Pumpkin' in the right order of events, including its lesson.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Retelling a fable means narrating its events in the correct order and ending with its moral lesson.
sla_notes_details: Pupils retell the story of the hare who tried to steal a bite of Mama Siti's giant pumpkin, found the skin too tough, was caught by Mama Siti, and learned that it is better to ask than to steal, making sure to keep the events in the correct order.
sla_notes_illustrations: A correct retelling begins with the hare admiring the pumpkin, followed by the attempted theft, being caught, and ending with the lesson learned.
sla_notes_daily_life: Retelling fables helps a pupil pass on moral lessons to younger siblings the same way elders tell stories in the community.
sla_exercise: What happened first in the fable 'Grandmother's Pumpkin'?::The hare admired Mama Siti's giant pumpkin and decided to nibble on it.||What happened after the hare bit the pumpkin?::The hare found the skin too tough and was caught by Mama Siti.||How does the fable end?::The fable ends with the hare apologising and learning that it is better to ask than to steal.

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Comprehend information presented orally
learning_activity_name: Retell oral texts
sla_name: Retelling a story to a partner and answering questions about it
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil retells a story to a partner and correctly answers at least three questions the partner asks about it.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Retelling a story to a partner and then answering their questions checks how well the story has been understood and remembered.
sla_notes_details: In pairs, one pupil retells a story they have heard, such as 'Road accident' or a fairy tale, while the partner listens and then asks questions about the characters, events and lesson of the story, after which the roles are swapped.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example question a partner might ask: 'What would you say if you had to tell a friend this story in one sentence?'
sla_notes_daily_life: Practising retelling and answering questions helps a pupil communicate news accurately when asked follow-up questions by family or friends.
sla_exercise: What should a partner do while you are retelling a story?::The partner should listen carefully and prepare questions to ask afterwards.||Give one example of a question a partner could ask after a retelling.::An example is: 'What lesson did you learn from the story?'||Why do we swap roles after retelling a story?::Swapping roles gives both partners a chance to practise retelling and asking questions.

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Construct meaning from simple texts
learning_activity_name: Read grade-appropriate texts to identify their basic components and contents
sla_name: Identifying title, characters and setting in a story text
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly identifies the title, main characters and setting of a read story.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Every story text has basic components such as a title, characters and a setting, which is where and when the story takes place.
sla_notes_details: Pupils read the story 'Grandmother's pumpkin' silently, then identify its title, the main characters (Mama Siti and the hare), and the setting (a small village and Mama Siti's garden), before discussing how these components help the story make sense.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example: the title is 'Grandmother's pumpkin', the main characters are Mama Siti and the hare, and the setting is a small village.
sla_notes_daily_life: Identifying title, characters and setting helps a pupil quickly understand and describe any storybook they read at home or in the school library.
sla_exercise: What is the title of the fable about a pumpkin?::The title is 'Grandmother's pumpkin.'||Who are the two main characters in the story?::The two main characters are Mama Siti and the hare.||Where does the story take place?::The story takes place in a small village, in Mama Siti's garden.

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Construct meaning from simple texts
learning_activity_name: Read grade-appropriate texts to identify their basic components and contents
sla_name: Identifying beginning, middle and end of a text
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly states what happens at the beginning, middle and end of a read text.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A text is organised into a beginning, a middle and an end, and identifying these parts helps a reader follow the sequence of events.
sla_notes_details: Pupils read the story 'Road accident' and divide it into its beginning (the writer's bus stopping and seeing an injured schoolboy), middle (a man finding the boy's exercise book and calling his father), and end (Baraka's father arriving and Baraka recovering in hospital).
sla_notes_illustrations: Beginning: the bus stops and a schoolboy is seen lying injured on the road; Middle: a man calls Baraka's father using a number in his exercise book; End: Baraka is taken to hospital and later discharged.
sla_notes_daily_life: Recognising the beginning, middle and end of an event helps a pupil narrate what happened during a school trip or family occasion in the correct order.
sla_exercise: What happens at the beginning of the story 'Road accident'?::At the beginning, the bus stops suddenly and a schoolboy is seen lying injured on the road.||What happens in the middle of the story?::In the middle, a man finds Baraka's exercise book and calls his father using a phone number written inside it.||What happens at the end of the story?::At the end, Baraka's father takes him to hospital and Baraka later recovers and is discharged.

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Construct meaning from simple texts
learning_activity_name: Read grade-appropriate texts to identify their basic components and contents
sla_name: Identifying the topic and key details of an informational text
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly identifies the topic and at least two key details of a short informational text.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: An informational text has a topic, which is what it is mainly about, and key details that give more information about that topic.
sla_notes_details: Pupils read a short informational passage, such as the interview text about a singeli musician and albinism, identify its topic, and list key facts it provides, such as statistics or explanations given in the text.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example: the topic of the interview extract is a singeli artiste and awareness about albinism, with key details such as the statistic that 75 people with albinism were murdered in Tanzania between 2000 and 2016.
sla_notes_daily_life: Identifying the topic and key details helps a pupil understand newspaper articles or notices posted at school or in the community.
sla_exercise: What is a topic of a text?::The topic is what the text is mainly about.||Give one key detail from the interview text about albinism.::One key detail is that albinism is caused by a lack of pigmentation in the skin, hair and eyes.||Why is it useful to identify key details in an informational text?::Key details give more evidence and information to support and explain the topic.

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Construct meaning from simple texts
learning_activity_name: Deduce the general meaning of a text
sla_name: Deducing the meaning of the story Road Accident
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly explains the overall meaning of the story 'Road accident' in their own words.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Deducing the meaning of a text means working out its overall message even when it is not directly stated.
sla_notes_details: Pupils read the story 'Road accident' and discuss what it shows about road safety and helping others, deducing that the story teaches the importance of being careful when crossing roads and helping an injured person quickly.
sla_notes_illustrations: Clues in the text, such as the man opening the bag to find identification and calling the father immediately, show the importance of acting quickly to help someone in an accident.
sla_notes_daily_life: Deducing meaning from stories helps a pupil apply lessons about safety, such as looking both ways before crossing a road, in their own life.
sla_exercise: What general meaning can be deduced from the story 'Road accident'?::The story shows the importance of being careful when crossing roads and helping others quickly in an emergency.||What clue in the story shows that people acted quickly to help Baraka?::The clue is that a man immediately searched the bag and called Baraka's father using the number found inside.||What lesson about road safety can a pupil learn from this story?::A pupil can learn to look carefully before crossing a road to avoid accidents.

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Construct meaning from simple texts
learning_activity_name: Deduce the general meaning of a text
sla_name: Deducing the moral lesson of the fable Grandmother's Pumpkin
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly deduces and states the moral lesson of the fable in one clear sentence.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Fables usually carry a moral lesson that is not always stated directly but can be worked out from the characters' actions and consequences.
sla_notes_details: Pupils discuss why the hare felt ashamed after being caught, and why Mama Siti forgave him, to deduce that the fable's moral is that it is better to ask for what you want than to take it without permission.
sla_notes_illustrations: The final line of the story, 'It's better to ask for what you want than to steal,' confirms the moral lesson pupils are asked to deduce themselves from the earlier events.
sla_notes_daily_life: This moral lesson encourages a pupil to ask before borrowing items from classmates or family members instead of taking them without permission.
sla_exercise: What moral lesson does the fable 'Grandmother's Pumpkin' teach?::It teaches that it is better to ask for what you want than to steal.||How did the hare feel after being caught by Mama Siti?::The hare felt ashamed and embarrassed.||Why did Mama Siti forgive the hare?::Mama Siti forgave the hare because he was honest and apologised for his mistake.

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Construct meaning from simple texts
learning_activity_name: Deduce the general meaning of a text
sla_name: Deducing meaning of unfamiliar words from context
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil correctly guesses the meaning of at least three unfamiliar words using clues from the surrounding sentence.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The meaning of an unfamiliar word can often be worked out by looking at the words and sentences around it, without needing a dictionary.
sla_notes_details: Pupils read texts such as the story 'Mr Fungo and the community' and guess the meaning of words like 'generous' from context clues such as 'he is always giving, whether it is time, help, or advice', then check their guesses using a dictionary.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example: the sentence 'Some people call him a generous man because he is always giving' helps a reader deduce that generous means willing to give freely.
sla_notes_daily_life: Guessing word meaning from context helps a pupil understand new words while reading newspapers or storybooks without stopping to look up every word.
sla_exercise: What does the word 'generous' likely mean, based on the sentence about Mr Fungo?::Generous likely means willing to give freely to others.||How can you find the meaning of an unfamiliar word without a dictionary?::You can look at the words and sentences around it for clues about its meaning.||What context clue in the text about Mr Fungo suggests he is kind?::The context clue is that he always helps and offers advice to make things better for everyone.

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Construct meaning from simple texts
learning_activity_name: Summarise issues found in the texts read
sla_name: Summarising the story Road Accident in a few sentences
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil writes a summary of the story 'Road accident' in no more than three sentences, capturing the main issue.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A written summary shortens a text into a few sentences while keeping only the most important information.
sla_notes_details: Pupils read the story 'Road accident' and write a short summary describing the main issue: a schoolboy called Baraka Musa was hit by a car while crossing the road, was identified through his exercise book, and was taken to hospital by his father where he recovered.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example summary: 'A schoolboy named Baraka Musa was hit by a car while crossing the road. He was identified from his exercise book, and his father took him to hospital, where he recovered.'
sla_notes_daily_life: Writing summaries helps a pupil record important events briefly in a diary or report to share with others later.
sla_exercise: Write a short summary of the story 'Road accident' in one or two sentences.::A schoolboy named Baraka Musa was hit by a car while crossing the road and was taken to hospital, where he later recovered.||What information should be left out of a summary?::Small unnecessary details, such as exact times or minor actions, should be left out of a summary.||Why do we summarise texts we read?::We summarise texts to show understanding and to communicate the main issue quickly to others.

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Construct meaning from simple texts
learning_activity_name: Summarise issues found in the texts read
sla_name: Summarising the fable Grandmother's Pumpkin
sla_assessment_criteria: A pupil writes a summary of the fable in one or two sentences, including its lesson.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH, PUPIL'S BOOK, STANDARD FIVE, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Summarising a fable includes stating both what happened and the lesson it teaches.
sla_notes_details: Pupils write a brief summary of the fable 'Grandmother's Pumpkin', mentioning that a hare tried to steal a bite of a pumpkin, was caught, and learned to ask instead of steal.
sla_notes_illustrations: Example summary: 'A hare tried to steal a bite of Mama Siti's giant pumpkin but was caught and learned that it is better to ask than to steal.'
sla_notes_daily_life: Summarising fables with their lessons helps a pupil remember and share good values learnt from reading with younger family members.
